title: Disk full, but df says 40% free
role: You are the junior on the ops rota for a PHP web portal on one Ubuntu server.

source.label: NADA issue #112: sessions folder pushes inodes to 100% (GitHub)

brief: Users of the data portal at `portal.example.com` get a blank page after login. The app log says it **can't write session data: No space left on device**. Priya, who set up the server, is sure the disk can't be full: it was resized last year.

steps.situation: You SSH in. `df -h` agrees with Priya: plenty of room. The error is real, though: new uploads and logins fail every time.
steps.evidence:
$ df -h /
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda2        78G   31G   43G  42% /
$ df -i /
Filesystem      Inodes   IUsed IFree IUse% Mounted on
/dev/sda2      5.2M    5.2M     0  100% /

choices.text: Check inodes on the same mount with df -i
choices.why: Each file costs one inode as well as some bytes. Millions of tiny files can use every inode while the bytes stay free, and `df -i` shows that in one line.

choices.text: Reboot the server, it clears temp files
choices.why: The files live on the root filesystem, not in RAM, so a reboot frees nothing. Users get an outage on top of the broken logins, and you have learned nothing.

Growing the disk adds bytes you don't need. ext4 fixes the bytes-per-inode ratio when the filesystem is made, so a grow adds inodes only in proportion, for the folder to fill again. You'd wait days for a change that only buys time.

choices.text: Delete old .gz logs in /var/log to make room
choices.why: A few hundred log files free a few hundred inodes, which the app burns in minutes. You also throw away history you may need.

steps.situation: Inodes are at 100%. Now find out where those millions of files are.

choices.text: Count inodes per directory with du --inodes -x
choices.why: It ranks directories by file count, not size, and `-x` keeps it on this filesystem. One directory holds 7 million files.

choices.text: Look for big files with find / -size +1G
choices.why: You are hunting the wrong counter. The culprit is millions of files of a few bytes each, which a size search never shows.

choices.text: Run ls -l in the app's files directories one by one
choices.why: On a directory with millions of entries, `ls -l` sorts and stats every one and can hang for many minutes.

steps.situation: `files/sessions` holds 7,057,174 session files (553 MB in total). They are old sessions nobody cleaned up. You need inodes back without breaking today's logins.

choices.text: Delete only old files with find -mtime +1 -delete
choices.why: `find -delete` removes files one at a time, so there's no argument-list limit, and anyone logged in today stays logged in (`-mtime +1` matches files at least two full days old). Check `df -i` as it runs.

choices.text: Sync an empty directory over it with rsync -a --delete
choices.why: The maintainer suggested this as a fast way to empty a huge folder. It works, but it signs out every user, so tell them first.
The shell expands `*` into 7 million names and fails with `Argument list too long`. Nothing is deleted.

choices.text: Delete the whole sessions directory and let the app recreate it
choices.why: Many apps don't recreate it, or recreate it with the wrong owner, so logins fail again with a new error. Empty the directory and keep it.

steps.situation: Inodes are back to 9%. Logins work. How do you keep this from coming back in six months?

choices.text: Daily cron cleanup, an inode alert at 80%, and a note in the runbook
choices.why: The app never deletes old sessions, so something else must. The alert catches the next growth source, and the note means the next on-call won't start from zero.

choices.text: Rebuild the filesystem with more inodes
choices.why: It needs downtime and a restore, and the folder still grows without limit. You've only moved the cliff.
The files came from normal traffic (later reports blamed crawlers). It will fill up again, probably at night.

debrief.what_happened: In August 2024 an admin of a NADA 5.4.1 data catalog reported that the root disk had free space but inodes were at 100%. The `files/sessions` folder held 7,057,174 entries, only 553 MB in all. A maintainer explained that NADA keeps session files there and does not clean up old ones. The advice was to empty the folder and add a cron job that deletes files older than one day. Because `rm -rf` on that many files could take an hour or more, the maintainer suggested syncing an empty folder over it with `rsync --delete`. A second admin hit the same problem in 2025, blamed crawlers and bots, and asked for the install guide to cover the cron job.
lessons: `No space left on device` can mean bytes or inodes: run df -h and df -i.
Rank directories with du --inodes -x, and never ls -l a folder of millions.
Anything that creates a file per request needs a cleanup job and an owner.
Alert on inode use as well as disk use.
